procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 29, 1964 of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 386 of 1963 (incorrectly referenced as 385 of 1963 in the text).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Judicial Magistrate overruled appellant's objections.
2. Appellant took the matter in revision to the Sessions Judge of Mehsana.
3. Sessions Judge referred the matter to the High Court in Criminal Reference No. 14 of 1962.
4. High Court ordered that the complaint under s. 182, Indian Penal Code was bad but directed the trial court to decide whether the appellant was removable from his office save with the sanction of the Central Government.
5. Judicial Magistrate held that the appellant was not removable from his office save with the sanction of the Central Government and the complaint should be rejected.
6. The first respondent preferred a revision petition before the Sessions Judge of Mehsana who dismissed it.
7. The first respondent took the matter in revision to the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 385 of 1963.
8. The High Court held that the appellant being an officiating Class I Officer was removable by the Railway Board and no sanction of Central Government was necessary and directed that the case under ss. 166 and 167, Indian Penal Code should proceed against the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (original defendant) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave because the Gujarat High Court overturned the Sessions Court and Judicial Magistrate's decisions, allowing the prosecution against him to proceed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a public servant 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government' within the meaning of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, thus requiring the sanction of the Central Government for his prosecution.

facts: The appellant was a public servant working for the Western Railway.
At the time of the complaint, he held a substantive post as a Class II Officer but was officiating in a senior scale as a Class I Officer.

He was prosecuted for offences under the Indian Penal Code, and he argued that the prosecution was invalid without the sanction of the Central Government as required by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
law: Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code requires prior sanction from the Central Government to prosecute a public servant who is "not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government."
The Railway Board Act, 1905, indicates that the Railway Board is a separate entity from the Central Government and derives its powers through delegation from the Central Government.
The legal maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se' means 'he who acts through another does the act himself.'
application: The Court first determined that the authority competent to remove the appellant from his officiating Class I position was the Railway Board, not the Central Government (i.e., the President).

The appellant argued that the Railway Board was essentially part of the Central Government. The Court rejected this, stating that the Railway Board Act shows it is a separate body exercising powers delegated to it.

The appellant then argued that even if the Railway Board was a delegate, the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' should apply, making removal by the Board equivalent to removal by the Central Government.

The Court rejected this argument as well. It held that once the Central Government delegates its power of removal to another authority (like the Railway Board), the public servant is no longer considered 'not removable... except by... the Central Government' for the purposes of Section 197. Citing a previous case, the Court reasoned that accepting this argument would improperly expand the protection of Section 197 to a wider class of officers than the legislature intended.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since the appellant was removable by the Railway Board—a separate body acting under delegated authority—he was not a public servant 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government.' Therefore, the protection under Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code did not apply, and no sanction from the Central Government was required for his prosecution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' applies when the Central Government has delegated its power of removal, meaning the public servant is still deemed removable only by the Central Government for the purposes of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: The Central Government had delegated its power regarding the appointment and removal of a public servant to another authority (in this case, the Railway Board).
The appellant, a public servant removable by the Railway Board, argued that he should still be considered removable only by the Central Government.
The appellant based this argument on the legal maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se', which means 'he who acts through another acts himself'.
law: Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides protection from prosecution without sanction to public servants who are "not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government".
The legal maxim at issue was 'qui facit per alium facit per se'.

The Court referenced the precedent set in *Afzalur Rahman v. The King Emperor*, which held that an officer dismissible by a delegated authority (a Deputy Inspector-General of Police) was not considered removable only by the Provincial Government for the purposes of Section 197.
application: The Supreme Court found that there was "no substance" in the appellant's argument and explicitly rejected it.

The Court established a clear rule: once the Central Government delegates its power of removal to another authority, the public servant is no longer considered "removable only by... the Central Government" for the purposes of Section 197.

The Court reasoned that applying the maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se' in this context would ignore the legislative policy of limiting the class of officers entitled to the protection of Section 197.

Following the logic of *Afzalur Rahman*, the Court held that the power to appoint and dismiss is vested in the authority to which it has been delegated. Therefore, the appellant was removable by the Railway Board, not the Central Government.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' does not apply. Once the Central Government delegates its power of removal to another authority, the public servant is considered removable by that delegated authority, not the Central Government, for the purposes of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a public servant 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government' within the meaning of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, thus requiring the sanction of the Central Government for his prosecution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that he was a public servant who could not be removed from his office without the sanction of the Central Government.
Consequently, he argued that the complaint against him was not maintainable without the sanction required under Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
To support this, the appellant's counsel relied on the Note to Rule 1704 and Rule 1705 of the Railway rules.
respondent_arguments: The rules cited by the appellant, specifically the Note to Rule 1704, were not applicable as they pertained to non-gazetted staff, whereas the appellant was a gazetted officer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' applies when the Central Government has delegated its power of removal, meaning the public servant is still deemed removable only by the Central Government for the purposes of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: It was suggested that even if the Railway Board had the delegated power to remove the appellant, this power was exercised on behalf of the Central Government.

Therefore, based on the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' (he who acts through another acts himself), the removal is effectively by the Central Government, making its sanction necessary under Section 197.
respondent_arguments: The delegation of power to the Railway Board was effective and complete, making the Railway Board the competent authority for removal.

The legal principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' does not override the specific statutory delegation of power, meaning the appellant was not removable by the Central Government for the purposes of Section 197.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If the Central Government has delegated its power to another authority with regard to the appointment and removal of a public servant, then for the purpose of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the public servant concerned will not be treated as a public servant 'not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government'.
obiter: The competent authority in the case of a railway servant officiating in a higher post, shall be determined with reference to the officiating post held by him at the time of taking action.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When the Central Government delegates its power to appoint and remove a public servant to another authority, that public servant is no longer considered 'not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government' for the purposes of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The act of delegation makes the delegate authority the competent body for removal, and therefore, the sanction of the Central Government is not required for prosecution.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of the phrase 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government' under Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code in the context of delegated authority.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' applies, stating, 'We do not think there is any substance in this argument.'

The court held that the delegation of power was legally effective for the purposes of Section 197, stating, 'If once th~ Central Govern- mert has delegated its power to another authority witit regard to appointment and removal of a public servant, then for the purpose of s. 197, Criminal Procedure Code the public servant concerned will not be treated to be a public servant "not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central G0vernment".'

The specific railway rules relied upon by the appellant (Note to r. 1704 and r. 1705) were found to be inapplicable, as they applied only to non-gazetted officers, whereas the appellant was a gazetted officer.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that the delegation of power to the Railway Board with regard to appointment and removal was effective, making the Board the competent authority for removal.
The court's reasoning aligned with the respondent's position that the legal maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se' does not override the specific statutory delegation of power in this context.

The court relied on precedent from Afzalur Rahman v. The King Emperor, which held that an officer dismissible by a delegated authority (like the Deputy Inspector-General of Police) was not a person 'not removable from office except by or with the sanction of the Provincial Government'.
policy_considerations: The court warned against interpreting the law in a way that ignores the legislative policy of limiting the class of officers entitled to the protection of Section 197, as doing so would create 'the danger of our ignoring the policy of the Legislature in limiting the class of officers entitled to this protection and of making s. 197, Criminal Procedure Code available to all public officers.'
